newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea to allow securities firms to issue bonds.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea to allow securities firms to issue bonds.

text.p: South Korea's finance ministry said on Sunday it would allow brokerage firms to issue corporate bonds from July as part of its financial reform plans.
The ministry said the ministry's plans were based largely on short-term financial reform proposals recommended in April by a presidential commission.
"We accommodated the commission's proposals as much as possible. But we set aside items that could cause disorder in the financial industry," the ministry said in a statement.
The commission's draft would generally free banks and non-banking institutions to engage in more kinds of business.
The ministry said securities houses would only be allowed to issue corporate bonds with a maturity of one year or longer within 400 percent of their shareholders' equity.
Securities firms would also be allowed to underwrite, trade and broker commercial papers from July under certain conditions.
Such bonds should be issued by listed companies with high credit ratings, the ministry said.

Banks would be permitted to issue financial bonds, but after consultations with other financial authorities, while insurers would be allowed to deal with foreign exchange business after a revision of relevant laws later this year.
The ministry said it would delay deliberation on the key issue of restructuring bank ownership until a revised bill on the bank law was prepared.

In the first phase of reforms, the commission recommended that each of the nation's top five business conglomerates, or chaebol, be allowed to have one non-permanent directorship on the board of a single bank.
Commission members agreed in April to limited chaebol participation in bank management, but decided to study further the question of chaebol ownership of banks.
